claims.text: An ultra-thin conformal nickel layer can be deposited by ALD onto tungsten surfaces before copper infiltration or sintering.
The nickel interlayer will enhance wetting between tungsten and copper.
The nickel interlayer will enhance interfacial bonding between tungsten and copper.
The nickel interlayer will reduce void formation in W–Cu composites.
The nickel interlayer will reduce phase separation in W–Cu composites.
Spark-plasma-sintered or mechanically alloyed W–Cu materials typically exhibit nonuniform interfaces, voids, and phase separation that impair thermal conductivity.
The nickel interlayer functions as an interfacial diffusion barrier.
The nickel interlayer promotes gradual chemical and structural integration between tungsten and copper.
Nickel lowers the interfacial energy between tungsten and copper.
Lower W–Cu interfacial energy improves copper wetting during infiltration.
A more uniform W–Cu interface provides better thermal connectivity.
A more uniform W–Cu interface increases resistance to mechanical degradation under fusion-relevant conditions.
Ni-coated samples will have a lower void fraction than otherwise identically processed uncoated W–Cu controls.
Ni-coated samples will have higher effective thermal conductivity than otherwise identically processed uncoated W–Cu controls.
Ni-coated samples will have greater mechanical durability, including higher yield strength and resistance to irradiation-induced degradation, than uncoated controls.
An ultra-thin nickel layer is needed to avoid formation of brittle Ni–W or Ni–Cu intermetallic compounds.
The proposed benefits will persist at high temperature and under irradiation in fusion-reactor components.
The optimal nickel-layer thickness and its long-term chemical stability under intense neutron irradiation are undetermined.
